newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait takes cautious approach on Islamic law.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait takes cautious approach on Islamic law.

text.p: Kuwait is gradually enforcing Sharia Islamic law but local politicians and Western diplomats doubt the Gulf Arab state will copy Saudi Arabia's public beheadings and strict dress code for women.

Kuwait's Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah announced in February that the task of making all laws conform with Sharia had been given to the country's Higher Consultative Committee. The extent of implementing Sharia varies among Moslem states.
"The Committee is proceeding with determination to realise the dream of all of us that we should be under the shelter of God's law," he said.
The panel, grouping a wide range of views, looks at legislation for any disparity with Islam and proposes amendments rather than devising new laws for immediate introduction.
ISLAMIC BANKING MEASURES AS PART OF GRADUAL APPROACH
"The rationale behind it is to be gradual...without alarming the West or overturning the system," said a Western diplomat who described the committee's approach as "quiet pragmatic".
The committee was appointed by the emir after a Western-led coalition drove Iraq out of Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.

Kuwait is preparing a draft law to regulate Islamic banking. But experts doubt the oil-rich state would seek to transform the entire banking system along Islamic lines, which condemns interest rates as usury.

Islamic financial institutions "will operate under the supervision of the Central Bank, not a totally independent and different system but one which works alongside the existing one," said a Western diplomat.
Kuwait, a major exporter of investment funds, "needs to keep its links to international banking. There will be one system in Kuwait, one aspect of it will be Islamic," added the diplomat.
KUWAIT'S ISLAMISTS WORK WITH THE SYSTEM
Islamist legislators say voters gave them a mandate in October polls to introduce Sharia. Women, slightly more than half of some 720,000 Kuwaitis, do not have the right to vote or run for parliament.
Nasser al-Sanea, a moderate Islamist who heads parliament's finance committee, told Reuters the West should not be concerned by the introduction of Sharia.

"Yes, there is an Islamic trend in Kuwait but it is calm, rational...and appreciated by Western academics. The smart thing to do is (Sharia's) gradual implementation in a way the people can accept. Not by force."
In response to an MPs question, the government announced in March a plan to launch a new television station dedicated soley to the promotion of Islamic teachings.
Analysts say Islamist MPs, who hold almost a third of parliament's 62 seats, were working through the political system to achieve their aims.

Islamist bills included a law passed by the last parliament to end co-education over five years, a reflection of the gradualist approach. The new house will discuss measures ranging from amending the constitution to banning musical concerts.
A group of MPs, including speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun, have proposed a constitutional amendment to make Islam the "sole" source of law instead of the "main".
Such a change requires a two-third parliamentary majority and the emir's approval. A similar bid was rejected in 1994 and many expect this latest attempt to fail also.
There are no political parties in Kuwait which is the only Gulf Arab state with an elected house and a free press.
KUWAIT'S ISLAMIST TREND SEEKS GRADUAL CHANGE
Leading liberal MP Abdullah al-Naibari sees the Islamist trend as "a wave of religiousness" sweeping across the region, although in Kuwait it was not militant.

"You cannot tell women not to drive in Kuwait. They are 30 percent of the 180,000 (Kuwaiti) workforce. I do not think this will reach the point of implementing public beheadings and amputations of limbs of convicted criminals," he told Reuters.
